strengths: Clear and well-motivated empirical analysis (Section 2) showing spatial locality across attention heads and recency locality across decoding steps in reasoning tasks, which directly motivates the proposed design.

The proposed method (Unified Attention Head Selection + Stable Recency Window) is simple, training-free, and easy to integrate into an existing sparse-attention pipeline (TidalDecode), lowering the barrier to adoption.

Strong and consistent empirical results across two model scales (Qwen3-4B/8B) and four benchmarks (AIME-24/25, MATH500, GPQA-Diamond), with LessIsMore matching or exceeding full-attention accuracy at much smaller token budgets than all compared baselines, including the training-required SeerAttention-r.

Efficiency claims are backed by an actual custom-kernel implementation and measured decoding latency rather than only theoretical FLOP reduction, and the paper additionally shows that LessIsMore avoids the generation-length inflation that hurts competing sparse-attention methods (Table 1).

Useful ablations (Fig. 8, Fig. 9) isolating the contribution of unified head aggregation vs. head-specific selection and the effect of the recency window ratio, which support the design choices rather than just reporting end results.
Honest and fairly detailed limitations/future-work section (adaptive ratio, generalization beyond GQA, memory savings, native training) that does not overstate the contribution.
weaknesses: The method is incremental relative to TidalDecode: it primarily adds a cross-head aggregation step and a fixed recency-window allocation on top of an existing backbone, and the paper explicitly states it is bootstrapped from TidalDecode's layer schedule (full attention/selection/sparse layer split), limiting the technical novelty.

The core locality analysis in Section 2.2 is drawn from a single AIME problem at a single layer (Layer 4) with a single model (Qwen3-8B); it is unclear how consistent these locality patterns are across problems, layers, and model families, which weakens the generality of the motivating claims.

The reported end-to-end speedups (1.1x vs full attention, 1.13x vs TidalDecode) are fairly modest despite claims of 2x fewer attended tokens and up to 87.5% sparsity, suggesting the practical efficiency benefit may be smaller than the sparsity numbers imply; the union/aggregation overhead (implemented in plain PyTorch, not CUDA) likely eats into potential gains.

The efficiency evaluation (Section 4.3) is conducted on a different model (Llama-3.1-8B) than the accuracy evaluation (Qwen3-8B/4B), justified only as being architecturally similar; this substitution weakens the direct coupling between the accuracy results and the latency results presented as a unified system contribution.

The fixed recency ratio r=0.25 and the choice of selection layers are hand-tuned per model via a small needle-in-haystack calibration (Appendix A.1) rather than derived principledly, and adaptivity is left entirely to future work, which somewhat undercuts the training-free simplicity claim.

No variance/confidence intervals are reported for the pass@1 accuracy numbers averaged over 16/8 samples, making it hard to assess whether some of the reported accuracy differences (e.g., LessIsMore vs. Full Attention at higher budgets) are statistically meaningful.

The method still requires maintaining the full KV cache (selection-based, not eviction-based), so memory savings are not realized despite the paper's efficiency framing; this is acknowledged but limits practical significance for memory-constrained deployment.

Comparisons are limited to TidalDecode, Quest, and SeerAttention-r; other recent training-free or hybrid sparse-attention approaches for reasoning are not benchmarked, leaving the relative standing of LessIsMore against the broader current landscape less clear.

strengths: The paper is grounded in a clear empirical motivation: token-level visualizations (Figures 2-3) illustrating spatial overlap of top-k tokens across attention heads within a KV group and a stable 'recency window' effect across decoding steps in reasoning tasks.

The proposed method (Unified Attention Head Selection + Stable Recency Window) is simple, training-free, and easy to integrate into an existing selection-based pipeline (TidalDecode), which is a practical advantage over retraining-based baselines such as SeerAttention-r.

Reasonably broad accuracy evaluation across AIME-24/25, MATH500, and GPQA-Diamond on two model sizes (Qwen3-8B/4B), with consistent trends showing LessIsMore closer to full-attention accuracy than TidalDecode/Quest/SeerAttention-r at low token budgets.

Ablation studies (aggregation scheme comparison in Fig. 8, recency-ratio sweep in Fig. 9) attempt to isolate the contribution of each proposed component rather than just presenting end-to-end numbers.

Honest and fairly detailed limitations section acknowledging lack of adaptive budget selection, unoptimized union-operation kernel, retained full KV cache (no memory savings), and untested generalization to MLA/MoE architectures.
weaknesses: The core empirical claims (spatial locality, recency locality) are illustrated with visualizations from a single layer (Layer 4) on what appears to be one AIME problem; there is no aggregate/statistical quantification (e.g., average head-overlap ratio, recall vs. layer/model) across many problems, layers, or models to substantiate that these are general phenomena rather than an anecdotal case.

The efficiency evaluation (Section 4.3, Figure 7, Table 1) is conducted on LLaMA-3.1-8B 'as a reference' to Qwen3-8B based on matching parameter count and GQA architecture, while all accuracy results are reported on Qwen3 models. This substitution is not well justified and creates an inconsistency between the accuracy and latency evaluation, weakening the overall speed-accuracy narrative.

The reported end-to-end and decoding speedups are modest (1.1x vs. full attention, 1.13x vs. TidalDecode), and part of the claimed 'end-to-end' gain stems from a 7% shorter generation length rather than from the sparse-attention mechanism itself, so the intrinsic computational benefit of the proposed selection scheme is smaller than headline numbers suggest.

The method still performs full attention at the (few) selection layers and requires maintaining the entire KV cache in memory (acknowledged in limitations), so memory savings—one of the main motivations for sparse attention on long-generation reasoning—are not demonstrated at all.

Novelty is incremental: the two techniques (global union of per-head top-k, and a fixed-ratio recency window) are straightforward heuristic modifications layered on top of an existing method (TidalDecode) rather than a fundamentally new selection mechanism; prior works (DuoAttention, StreamingLLM) already explored head-specialization and recency-window ideas that this paper mainly recombines/tunes for reasoning.

Generalization is only demonstrated within the Qwen3 family (4B/8B); despite motivating the paper with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B in the introduction, no accuracy results are shown for that or any other reasoning model family, leaving the claimed generality of the locality patterns unverified.

No variance/standard deviation or statistical significance is reported for the pass@1 accuracy numbers despite averaging over only 8–16 samples, making it hard to assess whether the accuracy differences (especially the sometimes 'above full attention' results) are statistically meaningful or noise.

The recency ratio r=0.25 and the two-selection-layer configuration are fixed/hand-tuned hyperparameters carried over largely from TidalDecode's own tuning procedure (Appendix A.1) using a small-scale needle-in-haystack probe, raising concerns about how well these choices transfer to other budgets, models, or tasks beyond what was tested.

Implementation details such as the union operation being done in plain PyTorch (not a fused CUDA kernel) suggest the reported latencies may not reflect a fully optimized system, and it is unclear how the aggregation overhead scales with larger batch sizes or longer contexts.

strengths: The paper provides a clear, well-motivated empirical analysis (Section 2, Figures 2-3) that reveals concrete spatial locality (cross-head token overlap) and recency locality (stable recency window) patterns in reasoning-model attention, directly motivating the proposed method rather than being an incidental observation.
LessIsMore is training-free and simple to integrate into an existing selection-based pipeline (TidalDecode), making it practically appealing and low-cost to adopt.

Evaluation spans multiple reasoning benchmarks (AIME-24/25, MATH500, GPQA-Diamond) and two model sizes (Qwen3-8B/4B), consistently showing near-lossless accuracy at substantially reduced token budgets compared to strong training-free (Quest, TidalDecode) and training-required (SeerAttention-r) baselines.

The generation-length analysis (Table 1) is a valuable and underexplored angle, showing that inaccurate sparse attention baselines inflate reasoning length (e.g., Quest +103% tokens at K=2000), while LessIsMore keeps lengths close to full attention — this ties accuracy and efficiency together in a compelling way.

Ablations are reasonably thorough: comparison of aggregation schemes (unified vs. randomized vs. head-to-head) under different selection frequencies, and a sweep over recency window ratio with both attention-recall and correctness annotations, support the specific design choices (25% recency ratio, global aggregation).
Actual system-level implementation with customized kernels demonstrates real (if modest) wall-clock speedups, not just theoretical FLOPs/token savings.
weaknesses: The efficiency evaluation (Section 4.3, Figure 7, Table 1) is conducted on Llama-3.1-8B rather than the Qwen3 models used for the accuracy evaluations; while justified as an architecture-matched reference, this creates an evaluation mismatch and leaves the actual end-to-end speedup on Qwen3 (the model used throughout the paper's headline accuracy claims) unverified.

The reported speedups are fairly modest (1.1× over full attention, 1.13× over TidalDecode end-to-end), which somewhat tempers the "efficient reasoning" framing in the title/abstract; it is unclear how much of the potential gain is left on the table due to unoptimized PyTorch-based union/aggregation operations (acknowledged in Sec 5.3) versus how much is a fundamental ceiling.

Generalization is narrow: all experiments use only the Qwen3 family (GQA) despite the introduction motivating the work with multiple diverse LRMs (DeepSeek-R1, Gemini, o3, gpt-oss); no results are shown for other model families or architectures (e.g., MLA, dense MHA), leaving open how much the observed localities and gains are Qwen3/GQA-specific — this is honestly flagged as future work but limits the current generality claims.

The method's novelty is incremental relative to its backbone (TidalDecode): it primarily contributes an aggregation/ranking scheme and a fixed-ratio recency window layered on an existing pipeline, rather than a fundamentally new sparse-attention algorithm; the selection-layer index and static ratio r=0.25 are hand-tuned via a small NIAH probe rather than derived principledly or validated across more models.

Memory savings are not realized (full KV cache still retained, as in TidalDecode), so despite the 'training-free sparse attention' framing, the main benefit is reduced compute/latency rather than the memory efficiency often emphasized in the broader KV-cache-compression literature — this is acknowledged but limits practical significance for memory-constrained deployment.

Statistical robustness of accuracy comparisons (e.g., variance across the 8-16 samples per benchmark) is not reported, making it harder to judge whether some of the reported accuracy differences among close competitors (e.g., LessIsMore vs. SeerAttention-r at higher budgets) are significant.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated empirical analysis (Figure 1, Figure 2) demonstrating that existing sparse attention methods (StreamingLLM, TidalDecode) suffer severe attention-recall degradation specifically on long-horizon reasoning tasks compared to retrieval tasks, providing a concrete diagnosis of the problem the paper addresses.

The identified structural properties (cross-head spatial locality and temporal recency locality) are intuitive, empirically supported with visualizations across layers/steps (Section 2.3-2.4, Appendix A.6), and directly motivate the proposed method's two design components.

The proposed method (CUSA + stable recency window) is training-free, simple to implement on top of an existing selection-based framework (TidalDecode), and architecture-agnostic (demonstrated on both GQA and MHA models).

Extensive experimental validation across multiple model families (Qwen3-4B/8B/14B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B) and reasoning benchmarks (AIME-24/25, MATH500, GPQA-Diamond), showing consistent accuracy improvements at aggressive sparsity levels (e.g., lossless accuracy at 2K token budget on AIME-24).

Notably avoids the generation-length inflation problem observed in prior sparse-attention baselines, which is an important practical finding (Table 2) since length inflation can offset any latency gains from sparsity.
Solid efficiency validation, including custom kernel-level benchmarks and realistic end-to-end serving evaluation in SGLang with FlashInfer, going beyond synthetic latency numbers.

Thorough set of ablations (recency ratio, re-selection layer choice, aggregation scheme, GQA-specific validation) that support the design choices rather than presenting them as unmotivated heuristics.
Additional generalization experiments to long-context (non-reasoning) tasks (NIAH, LongBench) and to an MHA-based model, strengthening claims of broader applicability.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution—aggregating per-head top-k proposals into a global ranking plus a fixed-ratio recency window—is a relatively incremental combination of ideas already present in prior work (StreamingLLM's recency window, TidalDecode's selection-then-reuse framework); the main novelty is largely empirical characterization rather than a new algorithmic mechanism.

The explanation for why cross-head aggregation preserves recall and generalizes across future layers is primarily supported by qualitative heatmap visualizations (Figures 2, 9, 10) rather than a more rigorous statistical or theoretical account of the union-based selection process, e.g., no analysis of expected recall as a function of head overlap or budget allocation.

Because LessIsMore retains the full KV cache (selection-based, not eviction-based), memory footprint savings are limited relative to eviction-based baselines; the paper does not clearly discuss this trade-off or memory cost implications for very long-context deployment.

The fixed recency ratio r=0.25 is treated as a stable universal hyperparameter, but the ablation (Figure 8) is conducted only on a single model/task combination (Qwen3-8B/AIME-24); it is unclear whether this ratio transfers robustly across models, tasks, and token budgets, especially given that GPQA and MATH500 have different reasoning length profiles.

The efficiency gains, while real, are modest at shorter context lengths (e.g., only ~1.1x at 16K context) and grow substantially only at longer contexts (64K); the practical impact for typical AIME/MATH problem lengths (~15-20K tokens per the paper's own data) is therefore more limited than the headline 1.6x number suggests.

The baseline comparison is somewhat narrow, focusing mainly on TidalDecode, Quest, StreamingLLM, and SeerAttention-r; other recent training-free or hybrid reasoning-specific sparse-attention approaches are not benchmarked, limiting the strength of the significance claim relative to the broader landscape.

The paper inherits its comparison layer-selection procedure directly from TidalDecode's own methodology, which, while argued to be fair, means the overall system design is tightly coupled to and dependent on TidalDecode's amortization structure rather than presenting a fully independent architecture.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: efficient long-horizon decoding for reasoning LLMs, where standard sparse attention methods are known to degrade accuracy.

The motivating analysis (Figures 1-2, attention recall curves) convincingly illustrates that existing per-head/per-step sparse selection methods (StreamingLLM, TidalDecode) suffer recall degradation specifically on long reasoning traces compared to retrieval tasks, providing a reasonable empirical motivation for the proposed design.

Broad empirical evaluation across multiple model families (Qwen3-4B/8B/14B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B) and several reasoning benchmarks (AIME-24/25, MATH500, GPQA-Diamond), plus additional long-context/retrieval experiments (NIAH, LongBench) and an MHA model (LongChat), supporting generalization claims.
Reasonably thorough ablations (recency ratio r, re-selection layer choice, GQA aggregation strategy, generation-length inflation analysis) that help justify individual design choices.

Practical systems contribution: kernel-level implementation with FlashInfer/SGLang integration and reported FLOP/memory/latency breakdowns, which is useful for reproducibility and real-world relevance.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the method is essentially TidalDecode plus cross-head aggregation and a proportional recency window; both ideas (recency windows, index reuse/amortized selection) have precedents (StreamingLLM, TidalDecode itself reuses selection across layers), making the core contribution incremental rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The central claim that 'token importance is global and stable across heads' is supported mainly by qualitative visualizations (a handful of heatmaps at selected layers/steps, Figures 2, 9, 10) rather than systematic quantitative metrics (e.g., average pairwise Jaccard overlap across heads/layers/models with confidence intervals), weakening the evidentiary basis for the paper's key insight.

Internal inconsistency: the abstract/introduction states LessIsMore uses 'two CUSA layers' to amortize selection cost, while the experimental setup (Section 4.1) explicitly uses only a single CUSA/selection layer for all comparisons — this discrepancy is not reconciled and raises reproducibility concerns.

At the token-selection layers, LessIsMore still computes full (dense) attention (Algorithm 1, line 10) to obtain scores for ranking, meaning true sparsity/speedup benefits are diluted at those layers; the paper does not clearly quantify how much this undermines the practical compute savings relative to a method that estimates importance more cheaply.

Reported end-to-end speedups are modest and context-length dependent (1.09–1.1× at 16K, scaling to 1.6× only at 64K), yet the paper's own data shows most AIME/GPQA/MATH problems are solved within 15–18K tokens under full attention — meaning the realistic speedup for the primary target workload (reasoning benchmarks) is likely closer to the lower end (~1.1×), which is understated in the abstract's headline '1.6×' claim.

Missing comparison to closely related reasoning-focused KV-compression baselines explicitly cited in Related Work (e.g., R-KV, Cai et al. 2025), which would be a more direct and recent point of comparison than SeerAttention-r or Quest.

The paper truncates the code availability statement ('Code is available at' with no link/footnote shown), and the Impact Statement is boilerplate with no substantive discussion of limitations, failure cases, or potential risks (e.g., scenarios where reasoning requires sparse, non-recent, non-globally-salient tokens, such as rare long-range dependencies).

Fixed hyperparameters (r=0.25, 4 attention sinks, specific re-selection layers chosen via a small needle-in-haystack search) are tuned per model family but presented as a general, principled design; the sensitivity of results to these choices across more diverse tasks/domains (e.g., coding, agentic workflows) is not explored, limiting confidence in broader applicability.

Evaluation is restricted to models up to 14B parameters; no evidence is provided for larger-scale reasoning models (e.g., 32B–70B+) that are more representative of real deployment settings where decoding efficiency matters most.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated empirical insight: the paper identifies and visually/quantitatively demonstrates cross-head spatial locality and temporal recency locality in reasoning model attention, which directly motivates the method design rather than being a post-hoc justification.

The proposed CUSA mechanism is simple, training-free, and architecture-agnostic, making it easy to integrate into existing selection-based sparse attention frameworks (demonstrated on top of TidalDecode).

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple model families (Qwen3-4B/8B/14B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B) and multiple challenging reasoning benchmarks (AIME-24/25, GPQA-Diamond, MATH500), plus generalization tests to long-context tasks (LongBench, NIAH) and MHA architectures (LongChat), which supports the generality claims.

Strong ablation studies (recency ratio r, re-selection layer choice, aggregation strategy under infrequent vs. frequent re-selection) that directly validate the design choices rather than treating them as arbitrary hyperparameters.

Practical efficiency contribution: kernel-level implementation with FlashInfer/SGLang integration showing consistent, non-trivial end-to-end speedups (up to 1.6x) and reduced memory transfer, going beyond a purely algorithmic contribution.

The analysis of generation-length inflation under sparse attention (Table 2) is a useful and underexplored angle showing that poor token selection not only hurts accuracy but also increases compute via longer traces—strengthening the paper's motivation and practical relevance.
weaknesses: The core observations (cross-head similarity, recency locality) are demonstrated mainly through qualitative visualizations (heatmaps) on a small number of cases (specific layers/models/steps); more systematic quantitative statistics (e.g., averaged overlap metrics across many layers/heads/steps with variance) would make the 'stable and global' claims more rigorous.

Comparisons are restricted to one choice of re-selection layer per model (though justified via NIAH search), and the method is only instantiated on top of TidalDecode; it's unclear how CUSA would perform if layered onto other selection-based baselines (e.g., Quest), limiting evidence for the claimed architecture-agnostic generality.

The method still relies on a hyperparameter r (recency ratio) fixed at 0.25 across all models/tasks without a principled way to set it other than empirical sweep; limited discussion of sensitivity/robustness of this single global value across different problem types or budgets beyond the ablation on one model.

Baseline comparisons for SeerAttention-r and Quest might not be perfectly tuned per-model since they're taken from original configurations rather than being optimized the same way as TidalDecode/LessIsMore (which share re-selection layer tuning), raising minor fairness concerns about baseline strength.

The efficiency gains, while positive, are relatively modest at shorter context lengths (e.g., 1.09x-1.1x at 16K) and the headline 1.6x number is only realized at 64K context, which may not be the most common practical reasoning-length regime; broader context-length coverage or discussion of when gains become significant would help.

Limited discussion of limitations and failure cases: the Impact Statement is essentially boilerplate, and there is no discussion of potential degradation scenarios (e.g., extremely long CoT tasks beyond 32K, multi-turn or agentic settings) or memory overhead/latency of the full-attention token-selection layers themselves at very long contexts.
